title: The Assertive Nationalists and the Partition of Bengal
tagline: Lal, Bal, Pal and Aurobindo: the Extremist challenge, its methods, repression and reunion.

overview.intro: The years between 1905 and 1919 produced the first open challenge to the Moderate method, when leaders impatient with petitions demanded swaraj as a birthright and were prepared to court arrest for it. This chapter explains what the Assertive or Extremist leaders stood for and what they opposed, works through the personalities of Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal and Aurobindo Ghosh, gives the partition of Bengal as the occasion for the movement, and then follows swadeshi and boycott, the repression that followed, and the reunion of the two wings at Lucknow in 1916. The key examination discipline is to keep the Moderates and the Extremists in separate columns and never to attribute one wing’s slogan to the other.

facts.label: The trio
facts.value: Lala Lajpat Rai of Punjab, Bal Gangadhar Tilak of Maharashtra and Bipin Chandra Pal of Bengal, with Aurobindo Ghosh as the fourth of the group.

facts.label: The slogan
facts.value: Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it — the words associated with Tilak.

facts.label: The occasion
facts.value: The partition of Bengal in 1905 by Lord Curzon, which turned a policy into a movement.

facts.label: The reunion
facts.value: The Congress reunited at Lucknow in 1916, when the Extremists were welcomed back and the Home Rule League was begun.

learn.title: What the Assertive leaders stood for and opposed

blocks.text: The Assertives accepted the goal the Moderates had set but rejected their route to it. Where the Moderates wanted reform within the empire, the Extremists demanded swaraj — self-government, and in the strongest readings of their writing, complete independence. Where the Moderates trusted petitions, the Extremists trusted swadeshi, boycott and national education and were willing to use agitation, though not yet violence. Where the Moderates had faith in the sense of justice of the British, the Extremists argued that the British would concede nothing that was not wrested from them, and they criticised the economic exploitation of India as a matter of policy rather than as an accident. They opposed the partition of Bengal, the repressive policies of the government, the loss of Indian industries and the unrepresentative character of the councils, and they stood for the preservation of Indian culture and religion as sources of national strength rather than as obstacles to be apologised for. Their famous fourfold programme was swaraj, swadeshi, boycott and national education.

items: Stood for: swaraj, self-government and, for some of them, complete independence from Britain.
Stood for: swadeshi, the use of Indian-made goods, and boycott of British goods, schools, courts and titles.
Stood for: national education through institutions controlled by Indians, and the dignity of Indian culture.
Opposed: the Moderate method of prayer, petition and protest, which they called mendicancy.
Opposed: the partition of Bengal, the repressive measures of the government and the exploitation of Indian industry.
Opposed: any doctrine treating British rule as a moral or civilising mission, insisting instead that it served British interests.

If British cloth, British schools and British titles were all withdrawn together, the economic and prestige cost of rule would rise, which was the logic behind the fourfold programme.

The use of goods produced in India and the encouragement of Indian industry as a lever of political pressure.

blocks.text: Lala Lajpat Rai, the Lion of Punjab, founded the Servants of the People Society, a disciplined organisation of workers devoted to national service, and led the agitation against the Simon Commission in 1928, in the course of which he was lathi-charged and died of his injuries. Bal Gangadhar Tilak, called the Father of Indian Unrest by the British, started the newspapers Kesari in Marathi and Maratha in English, was imprisoned for six years in Mandalay for seditious writing, and organised the Ganapati and Shivaji festivals to build a public culture of resistance; he was the most uncompromising of the four in his demand for swaraj. Bipin Chandra Pal, the articulate theorist of the Bengal group, edited The Sentinel and The Hindu and gave the boycott movement its most persuasive defence in speeches and writings, later breaking with those who turned to political violence. Aurobindo Ghosh, educated at Manchester and King’s College London, edited Bande Mataram and was acquitted in the Alipore bomb case, after which he withdrew from politics to Pondicherry and became a philosopher. Together they supplied the movement with its press, its organisations, its rhetoric and its willingness to go to prison.

items: Lala Lajpat Rai: the Lion of Punjab, founder of the Servants of the People Society, fatally injured at the Simon Commission protest of 1928.
Bal Gangadhar Tilak: editor of Kesari and Maratha, imprisoned at Mandalay from 1908 to 1911, and the clearest voice of swaraj as a birthright.
Bipin Chandra Pal: editor and theorist of the Bengali group and the most eloquent defender of boycott and swadeshi.
Aurobindo Ghosh: editor of Bande Mataram, accused in the Alipore case, later a philosopher at Pondicherry.
The group gave nationalism a press, a public festival culture and a doctrine of self-reliance in place of petitions.

learn.title: The partition of Bengal, Swadeshi and boycott

blocks.text: Lord Curzon announced the partition of Bengal in July 1905, dividing the largest province of India into two administrative units, and the official reason was administrative convenience in a province of nearly eighty million people. The Bengali public read it correctly as a division on communal lines, since Eastern Bengal and Assam had a Muslim majority while Bengal retained a Hindu majority, and the stratagem was understood as an attempt to break the unity of Bengali-speaking people and to weaken the centre of nationalist agitation. The response was immediate: 16 October 1905, the day the partition took effect, was observed as a day of mourning with rakhi tied on wrists as a symbol of unity, songs such as Bande Mataram were sung and processions filled the streets. The movement then turned to economics: swadeshi was preached, Indian cloth and indigenous manufactures were taken up, national schools such as the Bengal National College with Aurobindo Ghosh as its principal were founded, and a boycott of British goods, schools, courts, titles and honours was proclaimed. The government replied with prosecutions for sedition under Section 124A of the Penal Code, bans on processions, confiscation of newspapers and the Indian Press Act of 1910; the movement was also weakened when the partition was annulled in 1911, which removed the issue and, combined with the split in the Congress, allowed the government to recover.

items: The partition of Bengal was announced by Curzon in July 1905 and took effect on 16 October 1905.
Its effect was to divide a linguistic and cultural region on religious lines and to break the centre of nationalist agitation.
The response included the rakhi ceremony, days of mourning, processions and the singing of Bande Mataram.
Swadeshi encouraged Indian manufactures and swadeshi capital financed new mills, while boycott refused British goods and institutions.
National education produced the Bengal National College and a network of schools teaching in Indian languages.
Repression followed under the sedition law and the Indian Press Act of 1910, and the partition was annulled in 1911.

Swadeshi capital financed new textile and soap mills, which turned a political protest into an industrial movement with lasting consequences for Indian enterprise.

learn.title: The split of 1907 and the reunion of 1916

blocks.text: The differences between the wings turned into a rupture at the Calcutta session of 1907, where the Moderates, with the support of the chair, carried their own resolutions and the Extremists walked out; at the Surat session later that year the two groups could not even agree on the election of a president, the Congress split, and the government kept a close watch on both. Repression reinforced the division: Tilak was imprisoned for sedition in 1908, the Indian Press Act followed in 1910, and the mass movement in Bengal and Punjab was beaten down. The reunion came at Lucknow in 1916, where the two wings reconciled, the Pact of Lucknow settled the Congress-League relationship, and Tilak, who had come out of prison in 1914, moved the resolution welcoming the Extremists back. Two organisations of the period belong with the reunion: the Home Rule Leagues founded by Tilak and Annie Besant in 1916, which demanded self-government on the model of a dominion, and the nationalist press that carried the demand into every reading household. The reunion mattered because it joined the Moderates’ organisation to the Extremists’ mass appeal and gave the Congress the two wings it needed to enter the mass phase after 1919.

items: The split: Calcutta 1907, where the Moderates carried the resolutions, and Surat 1907, where the two wings parted company.
Repression accompanied the split: Tilak’s imprisonment in 1908 and the Indian Press Act of 1910.
The reunion at Lucknow in 1916, when Tilak’s resolution welcomed the Extremists back into the Congress.
The Lucknow Pact of 1916 with the Muslim League, settling a joint constitutional demand.
The Home Rule Leagues of 1916, founded by Tilak and Annie Besant, popularised dominion status as a demand.
The significance: organisation plus mass appeal, which prepared the ground for the mass movements after 1919.

items.note: Delegates could not agree on who should preside and the session broke up in confusion, which is why the split is remembered by the name of the town where it happened.
Founded in April 1916 with its headquarters at Poona, it organised public meetings and lectures that turned a constitutional demand into a popular slogan.

blocks.text: The honest assessment of the Assertive phase is that it changed what nationalism was, even though it did not achieve its immediate objectives. Its achievements were three: it shifted the emphasis from the councils to the country, bringing students, merchants, women and the urban public into political activity for the first time; it built the institutional infrastructure of a national economy and a national education system, however modestly; and it supplied the vocabulary — swaraj, swadeshi, boycott — that later movements reused almost unchanged. Its limitations were equally real: the movement remained largely urban and did not reach the peasantry except briefly in Bengal and Punjab, its economics was weaker than its politics so the mills that replaced British cloth were few, and the split of 1907 left the Congress divided for nearly a decade while the government recovered. The best judgement, and the one the marking scheme will accept, is that the Assertives failed in their immediate programme but succeeded in creating the mass methods and the spirit of self-reliance that Gandhi later organised, which is why their slogans and their leaders still head the chapters of the freedom movement.

items: Achievement: politics moved from petitions to the street, involving students, merchants, women and the urban public.
Achievement: swadeshi financed Indian industry and national education created an alternative to government institutions.
Achievement: the vocabulary of swaraj, swadeshi and boycott carried directly into the Gandhian movements.
Limitation: the movement stayed urban and did not organise the peasantry on a lasting scale.
Limitation: the split of 1907 weakened the Congress for a decade and made repression easier.
Judgement: immediate objectives failed, but the mass methods and self-reliance it preached made the later movements possible.

items.note: Name what was achieved in three points, what failed in two, then close with a judgement sentence linking the phase to the movements that followed.

questions.prompt: The slogan Swaraj is my birthright is associated with:
questions.explanation: Tilak made swaraj a claim of birth rather than a request for favour, which is the sharpest statement of the Assertive position.

questions.prompt: The partition of Bengal was announced by:
questions.explanation: Curzon announced the partition in July 1905 and it took effect on 16 October 1905.

questions.prompt: The Congress split into two wings in the year:
questions.explanation: The split followed the Calcutta session and was sealed at Surat in 1907; the reunion came at Lucknow in 1916.

questions.prompt: Which organisation was founded by Lala Lajpat Rai?
questions.explanation: The Servants of the People Society was a disciplined body of workers devoted to the service of the nation.

questions.prompt: The Assertive programme combined swaraj with swadeshi, boycott and national __________.
questions.explanation: The fourfold programme is the standard answer for what the Assertives stood for.

questions.prompt: Bal Gangadhar Tilak was imprisoned at __________ for six years for seditious writing.
questions.explanation: Tilak was sentenced in 1908 and released in 1911, which made him the most famous political prisoner of the age.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the methods of the Moderates and those of the Assertive leaders.
questions.answer: The Moderates relied on petitions, memorials, resolutions and speeches in the councils, trusting to the justice of the British and to gradual constitutional reform. The Assertives rejected this as inadequate and used swadeshi, boycott, national education and agitation, were willing to court arrest, and demanded swaraj rather than a share in the existing government. The Moderates worked among the educated elite, while the Assertives drew in students, merchants and the urban public.
questions.explanation: Petition against agitation, gradual reform against swaraj, and elite against public are the three contrasts to draw.

questions.prompt: Why was the partition of Bengal in 1905 opposed by the Bengali public?
questions.answer: The official reason given was administrative convenience, since Bengal was a very large and populous province, but the public read the division as a deliberate attempt to split Bengalis on religious lines: the new eastern province had a Muslim majority while Bengal retained a Hindu majority. It was also seen as a move to weaken Calcutta, the centre of nationalist agitation, by dividing the province that led it. Opposition therefore took the form of a day of mourning, the rakhi ceremony symbolising unity, and the swadeshi and boycott movements.
questions.explanation: The administrative reason against the suspected design of dividing Bengalis and weakening the nationalist centre.

questions.prompt: Mention two measures the government took against the Assertive movement.
questions.answer: The government prosecuted leaders and editors for sedition under Section 124A of the Penal Code, and Tilak was imprisoned in 1908 for six years. It also imposed the Indian Press Act of 1910, which allowed the confiscation of newspapers and the taking of security, and it banned processions and public meetings wherever the movement was strong.
questions.explanation: Any two of the sedition prosecutions, Tilak’s imprisonment, the Indian Press Act, bans on processions and the use of Section 124A.

questions.prompt: Describe the Swadeshi and boycott movements that followed the partition of Bengal and state their significance.
questions.answer: The partition took effect on 16 October 1905, and the day was observed as one of mourning: rakhi threads were tied as a symbol of unity, processions passed through the streets and Bande Mataram was sung. Political protest then took an economic form. Swadeshi was preached and Indian cloth, handloom yarn and indigenous manufactures were adopted in place of British goods; swadeshi capital financed new textile and soap mills; and boycott refused British goods, British schools, British courts and British titles and honours. National education supplied the alternative, with the Bengal National College under Aurobindo Ghosh and a network of schools teaching in Indian languages. The government replied with sedition cases, bans on meetings and the Indian Press Act of 1910, and many students and teachers were disciplined or dismissed. The significance of the movement lies in the three precedents it set: it brought students, merchants and women into politics, it demonstrated that economic pressure could be organised as a political weapon, and it created institutions — mills and schools — that expressed self-reliance in practice rather than in resolution.
questions.explanation: The response must cover the protest symbols, the practical strands of swadeshi, boycott and education, the repression, and the three precedents for later movements.

questions.prompt: Assess the achievements and limitations of the Assertive leaders.
questions.answer: Achievements: the Assertives shifted nationalist politics out of the councils and into the streets, so that students, merchants, women and the urban public participated for the first time instead of only the lawyers and professors who had dominated the petitions. They gave the movement an economic weapon in swadeshi, financed Indian mills and created national schools, which converted a cultural protest into practical self-reliance. They also supplied the vocabulary of swaraj, swadeshi and boycott, which the Gandhian movements reused almost unchanged, and their willingness to face imprisonment gave nationalism a moral authority that a privileged elite had lacked. Limitations: the movement remained urban and did not organise the peasantry except briefly in Bengal and the Punjab, so it never became the mass movement its rhetoric implied; swadeshi capital was too small to displace British manufactures and the alternative schools could not match the government universities; and the split of 1907 left the Congress divided for nearly a decade, which allowed the government to recover through repression and the annulment of the partition. The balanced judgement is that the Assertives failed in their immediate programme but succeeded in creating the methods and the spirit that made the later mass movements possible.
questions.explanation: Three achievements, three limitations and a closing judgement that links the phase to what followed.

questions.prompt: Why did the two wings of the Congress split in 1907 and why did they come together again in 1916?
questions.answer: The split arose from a genuine disagreement over method and goal. The Moderates wanted constitutional reform within the British empire and regarded swadeshi, boycott and agitation as reckless in a country where the government held overwhelming force and where repression would fall hardest on the students and merchants who took to the streets; the Assertives replied that petitions had produced little in twenty years and that swaraj could only be wrested, not requested. The disagreement became a rupture over organisation at the Calcutta session of 1907, where the Moderates carried the resolutions, and at Surat the two wings could not even agree on the election of a president and parted company. The reunion of 1916 was driven by changed circumstances: the First World War had shown the limits of British invincibility, Tilak had come out of prison and moderated his language, the Home Rule agitation under Tilak and Annie Besant had revived mass politics, and both wings recognised that neither petitions nor impatience alone could win self-government. At Lucknow the Congress welcomed the Extremists back and simultaneously concluded its pact with the Muslim League, so the reunion gave the movement both wings of strength — organisation and mass appeal — on the eve of the Gandhian era.
questions.explanation: Method against impatience explains the split, while war, changed leadership and the need for both wings explain the reunion.
